title: Why does nobody smile in old photographs?
subtitle: Pose, don't smile
subject: sciences
description: In 19th-century portraits, nobody smiles. Slow cameras get the blame, but the real reason lies in three centuries of portrait rules.
author: guido-manuel-de-la-torre-olvera

hero.hook: They are not unhappy, and the camera is not too slow: they are sitting for a portrait.

blocks.text: Photography started with a room, not a camera. The [[camera obscura]] is a dark chamber with a small hole: light passing through it throws an upside-down image of the outside world onto the far wall. Described in ancient China and studied by thinkers from the Greeks to Leonardo da Vinci, it shows the image. It cannot keep it.

Keeping it took until **1826**, when a French inventor, [[Nicéphore Niépce]], captured the view from the window of his house at Le Gras: the oldest surviving photograph from nature. He worked with bitumen, and the plate sat in the camera for **hours**. Niépce later partnered with another inventor, Louis Daguerre, who replaced the bitumen with a more light-sensitive resin. Even then, nobody sat for a portrait: nothing alive can hold still that long.

By **1837**, Daguerre had a working process: a silver-plated sheet sensitized with iodine vapor, developed over mercury vapor and fixed in hot salt water. This was the [[daguerreotype]]. The [[exposure time]] dropped from hours to minutes.

In **1838**, he pointed his camera at the Boulevard du Temple, one of the busiest streets in Paris. The photograph shows an empty city. Every carriage and every pedestrian crossed the frame too fast to leave a mark: the street looks swept clean of its people.

blocks.caption: Daguerre's Boulevard du Temple, 1838: at bottom left, the man having his boots polished.

blocks.text: Except one. A man who had stopped to have his boots polished stayed still for the whole exposure, and became the first human being ever photographed. He is in the picture because he was not moving. In **1839**, France bought the process and gave it to the world: the news was a sensation.

That same year, in Philadelphia, [[Robert Cornelius]] set up a camera outside his family's shop, uncovered the lens, walked into the frame and waited. The result is the oldest surviving photographic self-portrait: hair untidy, arms folded, eyes turned slightly to one side. He is not smiling.

This is where the usual explanation starts to fail. Lenses got faster, the chemistry improved, and within a few years a portrait needed **seconds**, not minutes. By the **1850s**, a photographer could catch a sitter in the time it takes to draw a breath.
So the faces should relax. They do not. For another **fifty years**, almost everyone who sat for a camera looked straight ahead with their mouth closed. Slowness no longer explains anything.

The real answer is that a photograph was not a [[snapshot]]. It was a portrait, and portraiture dragged **three hundred years** of rules behind it. Painters knew what a wide smile signaled, and it was not happiness.

blocks.caption: Malle Babbe, by Frans Hals (c. 1633-1635): in painting, a wide-open laugh went with madness or drunkenness.

blocks.text: [[Angus Trumble]], who wrote a history of the smile, puts it bluntly: a broad grin read as madness, drunkenness or stupidity. A saint might wear a faint one. A respectable person sitting for their likeness did not.
Teeth play a part too. For Angus Trumble, it is dentistry, not shyness, that eventually let people open their mouths in front of the lens.
So the first photographers copied the painters. You sat straight, you looked at the lens, you kept your mouth shut. What the picture recorded was the sitter's dignity, not their mood.

sections.title: They smile when nobody is posing

blocks.text: The rule was not absolute, and the exceptions give it away. An **1847** photograph of two officers from the Mexican-American War catches one of them grinning. An **1853** picture of a card game shows one player smiling while the other studies his hand. An **1860** portrait shows a man with his fists up, boxing, clearly enjoying himself.

None of these people were having their likeness taken. They were doing something, and the camera happened to be there. What changed everything was the snapshot. Cheap cameras put photography in the hands of people who were not sitting for a portrait, and by the **1920s** the smile had become the expected face.

blocks.text: We inherited that habit, which is why the nineteenth century looks so unhappy to us. It was not. It was striking a pose.
If nobody smiles in old photographs, it is not because cameras were slow: it is the rule of the portrait, inherited from painters, for whom a broad grin signaled madness or drunkenness.

sources.text: M. Fabry, « Now You Know: Why Do People Always Look So Serious in Old Photos? », Time, 28 novembre 2016.
